articles.title: CCTV, mobile data, Manipur trail: How police cracked Chennai's torso-in-suitcase murder
articles.summary: Chennai police say Odisha woman Hayathun Nisha was murdered for refusing abortion and pressing partner to marry; suspects arrested after suitcase body found on train.
articles.body: CHENNAI: A day after an Assam man and his wife were brought to Guduvanchery in connection with the murder and dismemberment of a 38-year-old woman, police said the victim was killed after she refused to terminate her pregnancy and pressured the man to marry her.Hayathun Nisha, 38, a native of Odisha, was murdered at a rented house on Mosque Street, Guduvanchery, earlier this month. Her dismembered remains were subsequently transported in a suitcase aboard Tamil Nadu Express.Guduvanchery police, using CCTV footage, mobile phone data and other technical evidence, traced Manik Uddin Laskar, 22, of Assam, and his wife Bhagabati Majhi, of Odisha, at Kashimpur in Jiribam district of Manipur on Saturday. The couple was arrested and brought to Guduvanchery on Sunday for further investigation.The murder came to light on Aug 5, when the Tamil Nadu Express, which had departed Chennai Central for New Delhi on Aug 3, reached Agra Cantonment railway station. Railway police checked an unclaimed suitcase in a general compartment found the dismembered remains of a woman inside.As the train had originated in Chennai, investigators began examining CCTV footage from Chennai Central and other railway stations along the route. Footage showed a man and a woman carrying the suitcase, and police subsequently traced their movements to Guduvanchery.The investigation eventually led police to the rented house on Mosque Street, where Nisha had been staying. Police said additional body parts were recovered from a large cooking vessel in the house. Investigators began probing her relationship with Manik Uddin, and found that Nisha had become pregnant and had been pressing him to marry her.She had refused to terminate the pregnancy, leading to frequent disputes. Police suspect Manik Uddin and his wife then decided to kill Nisha. After the murder, her body was dismembered and some of the remains were packed into the suitcase, which was taken to Chennai Central and placed aboard the Tamil Nadu Express, investigators said.During interrogation, the couple told police that Nisha’s head was shaved after it was severed. They initially tried to fit the head into the suitcase but, when they were unable to do so, smashed it into smaller pieces before packing the remains inside, police said. articles.title: Conheça os 11 distritos e 107 bairros de Mogi das Cruzes | G1
articles.standfirst: Cidade completa 466 anos nesta terça-feira (1º) e tem o território dividido entre áreas urbanas e rurais. Municípios vizinhos já integraram o território mogiano antes de se emanciparem.
articles.summary: Cidade completa 466 anos nesta terça-feira (1º) e tem o território dividido entre áreas urbanas e rurais.
articles.body:
Mogi das Cruzes conta com 11 distritos e 107 bairros — Foto: Mateus Costa/TV Diário

Mogi das Cruzes completa 466 anos nesta terça-feira (1º) com um território dividido entre áreas urbanas e rurais. Para organizar esse espaço, o município possui 11 distritos e 107 bairros (veja mapas abaixo).

🔎 A divisão administrativa reúne regiões com características próprias e passou por mudanças nos últimos anos. Taboão, Alto Parateí e Cocuera foram incluídos como distritos durante a revisão do Plano Diretor, concluída em 2019.

Mogi das Cruzes possui 11 distritos: Alto do Parateí, Biritiba Ussu, Brás Cubas, César de Sousa, Cocuera, Jundiapeba, Quatinga, Sabaúna, Sede, Taboão e Taiaçupeba (veja abaixo).

Segundo a Prefeitura, a definição dos 11 distritos ocorreu durante a revisão do Plano Diretor, realizada entre 2017 e 2019.

De acordo com o secretário municipal de Planejamento e Urbanismo, João Francisco Chavedar, o Plano estabelece regras para o desenvolvimento urbano e rural de Mogi das Cruzes.

Durante a revisão, a Prefeitura identificou crescimento nas regiões do Taboão, Alto Parateí e Cocuera. As três áreas foram incluídas na divisão distrital da cidade.

🔎 A criação dos três distritos ainda aguarda homologação e registro no Instituto de Geografia e Cartografia do Estado de São Paulo.

"O aumento do número de distritos demonstra a atenção da Administração Municipal com o potencial de crescimento de regiões da cidade e também o compromisso com a execução de ações que promovam este crescimento de forma organizada e sustentável", destaca Chavedar.

De acordo com a Prefeitura, os distritos têm características próprias e podem aparecer em mais de uma das quatro categorias definidas pelo município: indústria, comércio, serviços e agricultura.

⚙️ Industrial: Alto Parateí, Brás Cubas, César de Sousa, Cocuera e Taboão

🤝 Comércio: Brás Cubas, César de Sousa, Jundiapeba e Sede

🛠️Serviços: Brás Cubas, César de Sousa, Jundiapeba e Sede

🥬 Agricultura: Biritiba Ussu, Cocuera, Quatinga, Sabaúna e Taiaçupeba

Apesar das características próprias, os distritos também têm demandas em áreas como educação, saúde e transporte.

UBS do Alto Ipiranga, em Mogi das Cruzes — Foto: Divulgação/PMMC

Segundo a Prefeitura, todos os distritos da cidade possuem unidades de saúde, são ao todo 35, divididas entre Unidades Básicas de Saúde (UBS) e Unidades de Saúde da Família (USF).

Segundo a Prefeitura, todos os distritos têm unidades de saúde, sendo um total de 35, entre Unidades Básicas de Saúde (UBS) e Unidades de Saúde da Família (USF).

O distrito Sede concentra o maior número de unidades, com nove UBS e duas USF.

Os distritos com perfil agrícola, Biritiba Ussu, Cocuera, Quatinga, Sabaúna e Taiaçupeba têm o menor número de unidades de saúde. Todos contam com uma unidade, sendo uma USF em Biritiba Ussu, Cocuera, Quatinga e Taiaçupeba e uma UBS em Sabaúna (veja abaixo).

Além dessas unidades, Mogi também possui hospitais, Unidades de Pronto Atendimento (UPA) e Pronto Atendimento.

A UPA de Jundiapeba é a que registra a maior quantidade de atendimentos por mês, com cerca de 11 mil consultas (confira relação abaixo) .

Raio-x da saúde de Mogi das Cruzes — Foto: Cauê Adamuz/g1

CEIC Mundo Vivo em Mogi das Cruzes — Foto: Divulgação/PMMC

Mogi das Cruzes conta com 213 unidades de ensino municipais, entre escolas e creches. São 93 escolas municipais e 120 creches.

O distrito Sede concentra o maior número de unidades de ensino, com 40 creches e 31 escolas municipais.

Sabaúna e Cocuera têm o menor número de unidades de ensino. Cocuera possui duas escolas municipais e nenhuma creche. Sabaúna tem uma escola municipal e uma creche (confira)

Segundo a Prefeitura, todos os distritos possuem pontos de ônibus. Mogi das Cruzes tem dois terminais: Central e Estudantes. Os dois estão localizados no distrito Sede.

Mogi das Cruzes também possui quatro estações da Companhia Paulista de Trens Metropolitanos (CPTM). Estudantes e Mogi das Cruzes ficam no distrito Sede. Já as estações Brás Cubas e Jundiapeba estão localizadas nos distritos de mesmo nome (veja mapa) .

Infográfico - Estações de trem em Mogi das Cruzes — Foto: g1/Arte

Segundo o Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE), em 2026, Mogi das Cruzes tem cerca de 470 mil habitantes e área de 712,532 km².

De acordo com a Prefeitura, Mogi das Cruzes tem 129.559 imóveis registrados, distribuídos pelos 11 distritos.

O distrito Sede é o mais populoso e concentra o maior número de imóveis. Sabaúna tem o menor número de habitantes, enquanto Quatinga tem o menor número de moradias (confira abaixo).

Os 11 distritos de Mogi das Cruzes reúnem 107 bairros. Segundo a Prefeitura, a divisão complementa a organização territorial do município (confira abaixo).

➡️ O distrito Sede concentra o maior número de bairros, com 37. Em seguida estão Brás Cubas, com 19; Alto Parateí, com 11; e César de Sousa, com 10.

Jundiapeba reúne nove bairros, enquanto Taboão possui seis. Biritiba Ussu e Quatinga têm quatro bairros cada. Taiaçupeba conta com três, e Cocuera e Sabaúna possuem dois cada.

A divisão territorial de Mogi das Cruzes também mudou ao longo da história. Municípios que hoje fazem parte do Alto Tietê já foram distritos de Mogi antes de se emanciparem..

De acordo com a Prefeitura, Suzano, Poá, Itaquaquecetuba e Ferraz de Vasconcelos já foram distritos de Mogi das Cruzes.

📖 Suzano se desmembrou de Mogi em dezembro de 1948. Poá obteve a emancipação em março de 1949. Itaquaquecetuba se tornou município independente em outubro de 1953, e Ferraz de Vasconcelos também se emancipou em 1953.

articles.title: Amid row, Chhattisgarh judge named as Rajasthan HC Chief Justice
articles.summary: JAIPUR: The Supreme Court Collegium recommended Justice Sanjay K Agarwal of Chhattisgarh HC as Chief Justice of Rajasthan HC late Monday, ending a nea.
articles.body: JAIPUR: The Supreme Court Collegium recommended Justice Sanjay K Agarwal of Chhattisgarh HC as Chief Justice of Rajasthan HC late Monday, ending a nearly yearlong stint under acting CJ Sanjeev Prakash Sharma as protests by lawyers over his functioning intensified. The Collegium also recommended Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati as CJ of J&K HC.Hours before the recommendation, Sharma decided to abstain from judicial work from Sept 1 to 5. Rajasthan HC administration issued an amended roster for the period, assigning PIL matters to court no. 3, comprising Justice Inderjeet Singh and Justice Sandeep Taneja.The move came as two Jodhpur bar associations extended their boycott of Justice Sharma till Sept 6, demanding he be kept away from judicial and administrative duties. Rajasthan HC Lawyers’ Association and Rajasthan HC Advocates’ Association of Jodhpur resolved to abstain from court appearances.The bars had decided to submit a memorandum to the President, PM, CJI Surya Kant and senior Collegium judges, seeking a permanent full-time CJ for Rajasthan HC and an immediate end to the “targeted file system” across the state.The confrontation followed three letters Justice Sandeep Mehta wrote to the CJI on Aug 2, 10 and 17, seeking Justice Sharma’s transfer out of Rajasthan. Mehta accused Justice Sharma of misusing administrative powers and interfering in case listing, and sought a CJ from another state.In Jaipur, lawyers gathered outside Justice Sharma’s courtroom, shouted slogans and staged a brief sit-in Monday. articles.title: BRICS motorcade rehearsal today: Traffic diversions at 22 points in Delhi from 11am to 3pm
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi Traffic Police has announced traffic restrictions and diversions across several parts of the city on Tuesday in view of the motorcade.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi Traffic Police has announced traffic restrictions and diversions across several parts of the city on Tuesday in view of the motorcade rehearsal for the BRICS Summit 2026. The restrictions will remain in place from 11am to 3pm on September 1, with traffic being regulated at 22 diversion points covering more than 35 roads.The rehearsal is being conducted ahead of the BRICS Summit scheduled to be held at Bharat Mandapam, Pragati Maidan, from September 11 to 13. The affected corridors include major roads in central and south Delhi, including Sardar Patel Marg, Mother Teresa Crescent, Teen Murti Marg, Akbar Road, Tees January Marg, Rajesh Pilot Marg, Subramania Bharti Marg, Mathura Road, Moti Lal Nehru Marg, Dr Zakir Hussain Marg, Africa Avenue Road, Satya Marg, Shanti Path, Janpath, Ashoka Road, Barakhamba Road, Tolstoy Marg, Ranjeet Singh Flyover, Niti Marg and Panchsheel Marg.Traffic will be diverted at key junctions depending on the movement of the motorcade. At Dinesh Nandini Dalmia Chowk, traffic towards Mathura Road and Tilak Marg will not be allowed, while motorists will be diverted through BSZ Marg, IP Marg and Delhi Gate depending on their destination. Restrictions will also be imposed at Ram Charan Aggarwal Chowk and Mir Dard Chowk.In and around Connaught Place, traffic towards C-Hexagon from Kasturba Gandhi Marg and Janpath will be restricted. Motorists heading towards central, north, west and east Delhi will be diverted through routes including Kali Bari, Shaheed Bhagat Singh Road, Panchkuian Road, Minto Road and Barakhamba Road.Further south, diversions will be implemented at Patel Chowk, RML Hospital, Dhaula Kuan, Moti Bagh and Brij Hoshiyar Singh Marg. Traffic from Dhaula Kuan towards Sardar Patel Marg will be restricted, with motorists directed towards Ring Road and other alternative routes. Vehicles travelling towards IGI Airport and Gurgaon will be diverted towards NH-48/Gurgaon Road.Several restrictions will also be imposed along Lodhi Road and Mathura Road, including at Madarsa T-Point, Lodhi Road/Amrita Shergil Marg, Max Mueller Marg, Maharishi Raman Marg, Arch Bishop Macarius Marg, Neela Gumbad and under the Oberoi Flyover.At Mandi House, traffic towards Feroz Shah Road, Bhagwan Das Road and Copernicus Marg will be restricted. articles.title: Scientists used geothermal drill-hole temperatures in Oregon’s Cascades and found at least 81 cubic kilometres of water hidden in volcanic rock, nearly 3 times Lake Mead’s capacity
articles.summary: US News: Beneath the forested slopes of Oregon’s Cascade Range, scientists have uncovered a vast, hidden reservoir of water locked inside volcanic rock. By ana.
articles.body: Beneath the forested slopes of Oregon’s Cascade Range, scientists have uncovered a vast, hidden reservoir of water locked inside volcanic rock. By analysing temperature data from geothermal drill holes, a University of Oregon-led team estimated that at least 81 cubic kilometres of water are stored in the region’s subsurface, nearly three times the capacity of Lake Mead, the largest reservoir in the United States. The discovery, announced by the university, reshapes how researchers think about water storage in volcanic mountains and could have implications for everything from regional water budgets to volcanic hazard assessment.A surprise hidden in old drill dataThe finding did not come from new drilling or expensive field campaigns, but from a fresh look at existing data. The team, led by University of Oregon geosciences professor Leif Karlstrom, focused on temperature measurements collected from geothermal exploration wells drilled decades ago across the Oregon Cascades.These drill holes were originally used to assess geothermal energy potential, not to map groundwater. But the researchers realised that the way heat moves through rock is strongly influenced by whether the pores and fractures are filled with air or water. Water conducts heat differently than dry rock, and those differences leave a detectable signature in temperature profiles.By modelling how heat should flow through dry volcanic rock and comparing it to the actual temperature logs, the scientists could infer where large volumes of water must be present.The result was a surprising picture of the subsurface: instead of mostly dry, fractured lava flows, the team found evidence for a regionally extensive, water-saturated zone stretching across a large portion of the Oregon Cascades.How much water are we talking about?The team’s calculations suggest that at least 81 cubic kilometres of water are stored in the volcanic rocks of the study area. To put that in perspective, Lake Mead, the massive reservoir formed by Hoover Dam on the Colorado River, has a full capacity of about 28 cubic kilometres. In other words, the hidden aquifer beneath the Oregon Cascades could hold nearly three times as much water as the largest reservoir in the U.S.This does not mean there is an underground “lake” that could be tapped like a surface reservoir. The water is dispersed through countless pores, fractures and vesicles (gas bubbles) in layers of lava flows, volcaniclastic deposits and other volcanic rocks. It is more like a giant, three-dimensional sponge than a single body of standing water.Why volcanic mountains can store so much waterVolcanic terrains are unusually good at storing groundwater. Repeated eruptions build up thick stacks of lava flows, ash layers and fragmented volcanic deposits. As these materials cool and weather, they develop: Porous zones where gas bubbles were trapped in solidifying lava; fracture networks created by cooling, tectonic stress and later erosion; and permeable layers of volcanic breccia and sediment between harder flows.In wet, high-elevation environments like the Oregon Cascades, abundant precipitation from rain and snowmelt can infiltrate deeply into these rocks. Eventually, this forms large saturated zones which can last for long periods, even during dry summers or multi-year droughts.Many previous models assumed that a large fraction of water in volcanic mountains either drained rapidly through fractures or was stored primarily in shallow soils and alluvial valleys. The new results indicate that a much larger fraction is stored in the volcanic bedrock itself, with important implications for water movement through the landscape.Implications for water budgets and drought resilienceThis finding raises a key question for water managers and hydrologists: How much of the precipitation that falls on the Cascades is stored in these deep volcanic aquifers, and how slowly is it released? If a significant portion of runoff is buffered by this hidden storage, it could mean that streams and springs are more resilient to drought than previously thought, supported by slow drainage from the volcanic aquifer. It also suggests that regional water budgets may need to be revised to account for larger subsurface storage and longer residence times. And climate change impacts on streamflow could be moderated, at least temporarily, by the slow release of water from these deep reservoirs.At the same time, the study underscores how little is still known about groundwater in many mountainous regions. The Oregon Cascades are relatively well studied compared to other ranges, yet a water store of this magnitude remained undetected until now.Connections to volcanic hazardsThe findings also matter for volcanology. Water plays a critical role in how volcanoes behave.When magma rises through wet crust, it can interact with groundwater, potentially triggering explosive eruptions or hydrothermal activity.Knowing that large volumes of water are stored in the volcanic edifice itself helps scientists better model: How heat and fluids move beneath active volcanoes; where hydrothermal systems are likely to form; and how eruptions might interact with subsurface water to produce phreatic or phreatomagmatic explosions.While the study does not change the overall hazard profile of Oregon’s volcanoes, it adds an important piece to the puzzle of how these systems are plumbed.A new way to “see” groundwaterOne of the most powerful aspects of this work is the method itself. Instead of relying solely on traditional groundwater monitoring wells, which are sparse in remote mountain areas, the team used existing geothermal temperature logs as a kind of indirect imaging tool.This approach could be applied in other volcanic regions around the world, from the Andes to the Japanese archipelago, where similar stacks of lava flows and abundant precipitation may hide large aquifers. It offers a relatively low-cost way to refine estimates of subsurface water storage in places where drilling new wells would be prohibitively expensive.What this means for the Oregon CascadesFor the Oregon Cascades, the study suggests that the landscape’s water cycle is more complex and more buffered than previously recognised. The forests, meadows and rivers that define the region are underpinned by a vast, slow-moving reservoir that helps regulate flow through wet and dry periods.The researchers emphasise that this is a minimum estimate; the true volume could be larger as more data are analysed and models are refined. Future work will likely focus on: Integrating the temperature-based estimates with streamflow, geochemical and seismic data; mapping how the aquifer varies across different volcanic centres and rock types; assessing how climate change might affect recharge and long-term storage in these systems.A hidden resource with big questionsThe discovery of 81 cubic kilometres of water beneath the Oregon Cascades is a reminder of how much remains unknown about Earth’s subsurface. While this water is not a direct source of drinking water or irrigation in the conventional sense, it plays a crucial role in sustaining ecosystems, streams and potentially even geothermal resources. As scientists continue to probe these hidden reservoirs, the challenge will be to understand not just how much water is there, but how it moves, how it interacts with surface systems and how it might respond to a warming, changing climate.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Stalked from garage for weeks, entered while she slept: Chilling details emerge in Hyderabad nurse's rape-murder
articles.summary: HYDERABAD: Police on Monday arrested a bike mechanic from Bihar for the alleged rape and murder of a nurse in Pahadishareef, saying he had been watchi.
articles.body: HYDERABAD: Police on Monday arrested a bike mechanic from Bihar for the alleged rape and murder of a nurse in Pahadishareef, saying he had been watching her movements for nearly a month before allegedly entering her room through a window while she slept.According to police, the accused, who came to Hyderabad in 2023 for work, was employed at a garage located close to the rear window of the room where the nurse lived. Investigators said he first noticed the woman through the window about a month before the crime and allegedly began monitoring her movements thereafter.Police said the accused entered the room through the window while the nurse was asleep and allegedly attempted to sexually assault her. She resisted, following which he allegedly strangled her to death before escaping through the same window.However, investigators said they could not conclusively establish whether the sexual assault occurred before or after the woman's death. The accused allegedly told police that she was unconscious when the assault took place.“Whether the victim had died by then or not cannot be ascertained,” an investigating officer said.Police said the accused was allegedly under the influence of alcohol when he committed the crime. After the incident, he reportedly returned to the garage and went to sleep. He initially denied involvement in the murder.Investigators subsequently analysed mobile phone tower data and other evidence and questioned him again, following which he allegedly confessed to the crime. Police also recovered hair strands and other forensic evidence from the scene.Investigators said the victim's belongings, including her mobile phone and headphones, were left untouched, suggesting that robbery was not the motive.The crime came to light when the woman's friend, unable to contact her, went to her room with a few others. Finding the door locked, they entered through the window and found her dead.The case was initially registered as a murder. Following the medical examination, police added sections relating to rape as well as provisions of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.The accused will be produced before a magistrate. Police are also checking with Bihar authorities to determine whether he has any previous criminal record.The victim had moved to Hyderabad from Kothagudem about seven months ago and was working as a nurse at a private hospital. articles.title: Laurene Powell Jobs left Wall Street and moved to Florence for eight months, then built a multibillion-dollar empire funding education, climate and social change
articles.summary: US News: Laurene Powell Jobs took an unconventional route from Wall Street to becoming one of the most influential philanthropists and investors in the United .
articles.body: Laurene Powell Jobs took an unconventional route from Wall Street to becoming one of the most influential philanthropists and investors in the United States. After graduating from the University of Pennsylvania in 1985, she spent a year at Merrill Lynch and two years at Goldman Sachs before leaving finance and moving to Florence, Italy, where she lived for eight months. She later returned to the US and earned an MBA from Stanford University in 1991. Her life changed dramatically after she married Apple co-founder Steve Jobs and later inherited a substantial fortune following his death in 2011. Rather than simply preserving that wealth, Powell Jobs channelled it into Emerson Collective, an organisation involved in education, immigration, climate, media and social change, turning her personal fortune into a far-reaching platform for influence.Why Laurene Powell Jobs left Wall Street and moved to FlorencePowell Jobs was born in West Milford, New Jersey, in 1963 and experienced financial hardship early in life after her father, a Marine Corps pilot, died in a plane crash when she was three. Her mother was left to raise three children, and Powell Jobs later recalled learning the importance of becoming self-sufficient. She attended the University of Pennsylvania, where she studied political science and economics, graduating in 1985. She then entered the financial world, working for a year at Merrill Lynch and two years in Goldman Sachs' fixed-income division. Although the experience gave her valuable exposure to finance, she eventually became dissatisfied with the sense that her work was not contributing enough to the wider world. She left Goldman Sachs and moved to Florence, where she spent eight months before returning to the United States and enrolling at Stanford Graduate School of Business. She earned her MBA in 1991, the same year she married Steve Jobs.How she met Steve Jobs and built a life beyond financePowell Jobs met Steve Jobs while attending a lecture he was giving at Stanford's business school. According to accounts later included in Walter Isaacson's biography of Jobs, the two ended up sitting beside each other and began talking. They went to dinner after the lecture and their relationship developed quickly. Jobs proposed on New Year's Day in 1990, and the couple married in 1991. They eventually had three children, Reed, Erin and Eve. Powell Jobs stepped back from a conventional professional career for a period to focus on raising her family, while also pursuing entrepreneurial and social-impact interests. She started Terravera, a small business producing organic meals, although the venture did not last. Her interest in education became more enduring. In 1997, she and Carlos Watson co-founded College Track, a nonprofit designed to help students from disadvantaged backgrounds complete high school, attend college and graduate. The organisation reflected a personal belief that education could fundamentally alter a young person's opportunities.Emerson Collective became the centre of her social-impact workPowell Jobs began laying the groundwork for Emerson Collective in 2004, years before Steve Jobs died. The organisation eventually became the principal vehicle through which she pursued philanthropy, investment and advocacy. Emerson Collective describes its mission around creating greater opportunity and addressing entrenched social problems, with work spanning education, immigration, climate change, media and other areas. Its structure is unusual because it operates as a limited liability company rather than solely as a traditional charitable foundation. That gives Powell Jobs greater flexibility to combine grants and philanthropic activity with investments in companies and other organisations. The model means her activities cannot be understood simply as charitable giving. Some of the money is directed towards nonprofits and social causes, while other capital is invested in businesses, media organisations and projects that align with her broader objectives. This approach has made Emerson Collective an unusually flexible instrument for deploying a vast personal fortune.How education became one of her biggest prioritiesEducation has remained one of the central themes of Powell Jobs' work. Her involvement began well before she inherited Steve Jobs' fortune, with the creation of College Track in 1997. The organisation works with students from communities that face barriers to higher education, supporting them through high school and college. She later backed other education initiatives through Emerson Collective, including XQ, a major programme focused on transforming high-school education in the United States. XQ has supported schools and educators seeking to rethink how high-school students learn and prepare for life after graduation. Powell Jobs has repeatedly argued that education needs new approaches and greater experimentation, drawing on the problem-solving mindset associated with entrepreneurship. Her own educational journey, from a financially constrained childhood to Penn and Stanford, has also helped shape the importance she places on creating opportunities for young people who might otherwise struggle to access them.Her fortune expanded dramatically after Steve Jobs' deathSteve Jobs died on October 5, 2011, after years of health problems. His death transformed Powell Jobs' financial position as she became the beneficiary of a substantial portfolio of Apple and Disney holdings. The precise value of her inheritance has varied over time and depends heavily on the valuation date, particularly because both companies' share prices have changed dramatically. Jobs had received a large Disney stake when Disney acquired Pixar in 2006, while the family's Apple holdings also represented a major source of wealth. Powell Jobs consequently became one of the world's wealthiest women. Her post-2011 activities showed that she intended to use that financial power actively rather than simply hold the assets. Emerson Collective expanded considerably, giving her the ability to direct capital towards causes and organisations while also taking positions in commercial ventures. Her wealth therefore became not just a private financial asset but a mechanism through which she could influence education, journalism, climate policy, immigration and other areas of public life.Why she invested heavily in mediaOne of the most visible parts of Powell Jobs' expansion has been her involvement in media. Emerson Collective acquired a majority stake in Atlantic Media, the company behind The Atlantic, in 2017. She also became involved with other media and entertainment ventures, including Pop-Up Magazine Productions and Concordia Studio, while investing in or supporting organisations involved in journalism and documentary storytelling. Her interest in media fits closely with her broader belief in the power of storytelling to influence public debate. Through these investments, Powell Jobs gained influence not only as a philanthropist but also as an important participant in the American media landscape. The strategy also reflects a distinctive feature of Emerson Collective's model. Rather than separating charitable activity from commercial investment completely, the organisation can use different forms of capital depending on the objective. That flexibility has allowed Powell Jobs to support journalism and storytelling while also participating directly in the businesses producing them.Climate change became another major focusClimate change is another major area in which Powell Jobs has directed resources through Emerson Collective. The organisation has supported efforts related to environmental protection, climate solutions and efforts to address the wider consequences of climate change. Her approach has generally involved backing organisations, entrepreneurs and initiatives that seek structural changes rather than limiting support to traditional charitable programmes. This fits the wider philosophy behind Emerson Collective, which attempts to combine philanthropy with investment and advocacy. The scale of Powell Jobs' wealth gives her the ability to support projects for long periods and to take risks that conventional funding models may not always accommodate. Her climate work therefore sits alongside her education and media interests as part of a broader strategy of using private capital to influence areas that she believes require significant change.She also became involved in immigration and social justiceImmigration and social justice have formed another significant part of Powell Jobs' public work. Emerson Collective has supported organisations working with immigrants and communities affected by policy changes, while Powell Jobs herself has spoken publicly about social inequality and political issues. Her involvement has extended beyond writing cheques, with the organisation supporting advocacy groups and initiatives designed to influence public discussion and policy. She has also used high-profile appearances and conversations with activists to bring attention to issues she considers important. This combination of funding, advocacy and media influence has made her considerably more visible than she was during Steve Jobs' lifetime. Before his death, Powell Jobs largely maintained a private profile and was often described publicly primarily in relation to her husband. In the years since, she has developed a distinct identity as a philanthropist, investor and advocate with considerable influence of her own.Powell Jobs expanded her influence beyond philanthropyHer activities have also reached the world of professional sport. In 2017, Powell Jobs invested a reported $500 million for a roughly 20% stake in Monumental Sports & Entertainment, the company that owns the NBA's Washington Wizards, WNBA's Washington Mystics and operates Capital One Arena. The investment added another major sector to her portfolio and demonstrated the breadth of her financial interests. Her influence has consequently extended across education, media, entertainment, climate, social policy and professional sport. Yet the scale of her activities has also attracted scrutiny. Because Emerson Collective is structured as an LLC, it has more flexibility and fewer disclosure requirements than a conventional private foundation. That makes it difficult for outsiders to determine the full extent of Powell Jobs' giving and investments. Supporters argue that the structure allows her to respond quickly to changing circumstances, while critics have questioned the transparency that comes with such a model.From Wall Street to a different kind of powerPowell Jobs' journey is unusual because her transformation did not happen overnight. Her decision to leave Wall Street and spend eight months in Florence came decades before she became one of the world's wealthiest women. Her early interest in education, her experience raising a family and her work with College Track all predated the enormous fortune she later inherited. Steve Jobs' death undoubtedly changed the scale of what she could do, but it did not create her interest in social issues from scratch. Through Emerson Collective, she has since combined wealth with philanthropy, investment, advocacy and media ownership in a way that gives her unusual freedom to pursue causes she considers important. Her story is therefore not simply about inheriting billions. It is about how a woman who once left finance because she wanted her work to have greater meaning eventually gained the resources to decide, on an enormous scale, what that meaningful work would look like.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Tunnels and tough terrain: Indian Army joins Nepal's flood rescue effort
articles.summary: News News: Technical teams of the Indian army have worked through difficult conditions in Nepal, joining hands with the Nepali Army at the Chilime and Langtang t.
articles.body: Technical teams of the Indian army have worked through difficult conditions in Nepal, joining hands with the Nepali Army at the Chilime and Langtang tunnel sites as part of an ongoing search and rescue operation following flash floods that hit the region. At Chilime, the team managed to establish a foothold at the tunnel entrance and set up safety ropes inside despite poor weather and hard terrain access. At Langtang, the joint team probed 185 metres into the tunnel, working alongside Nepali forces in what has been a slow, careful search given the unstable conditions inside.The deployment came at Nepal's request, with India sending specialised personnel trained for tunnel search and rescue, work that demands both technical skill and physical stamina given the confined and often unstable spaces involved. This is not new territory for the two militaries. India and Nepal have coordinated on disaster response for years, and officials say that experience showed in how smoothly the two teams worked together on the ground this time. The army and the air force had relentlessly worked in what are called Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) operations after the 2015 earthquake that had leveled parts of Nepal's capital and had caused wide spread damage across the country. The ministry of external affairs has also issued helpline numbers for Indian nationals stuck in Nepal.India's Ambassador to Nepal Naveen Srivastava travelled to the Nepali Army's base in Bidur, Nuwakot, which is functioning as the main staging point for rescue and relief work in Rasuwa district. There, he met the Indian technical teams handling the Langtang and Chilime operations and was briefed on their progress so far, as well as the obstacles still ahead. The ambassador also met Nepal's Home Minister and the Minister for Energy and Water Resources during the visit, with discussions understood to have covered relief logistics and the overall extent of the flood damage.Rescue work is set to continue over the coming days. The operation is the latest example of a disaster response relationship between India and Nepal that goes back years. The army had also participated in tunnel rescue operations in the past. The Corps of Engineers of the army took part in the rescue operations that took over two weeks and saw the successful rescue of 41 trapped workers. The army, due to its operations in mountainous regions of the high Himalayas has acquired an expertise in operating in the difficult mountainous terrain.

articles.title: Upcoming cars in September 2026: Kia Sorento, BMW 7 Series & more
articles.summary: Cars News: September is set to bring more new car launches and updates to the Indian market, following a busy August that saw several new models, variants and up.
articles.body: September is set to bring more new car launches and updates to the Indian market, following a busy August that saw several new models, variants and updates. Last month, the BMW X1 LWB and MG Hector Tomahawk EV and PHEV launched, while the Mahindra Scorpio N received a mid-lifecycle update. The Mahindra BE 6 also gained the ‘Sporteq’ suffix, and three existing models - the Range Rover SV Ultra, BYD Sealion 7 Dynamic and Skoda Kylaq Sportline received new trims. With more launches lined up for September, buyers can expect new options across multiple segments. Here’s a look at the cars expected to arrive in India this month.Kia SorentoKia will add the Sorento as its new flagship ICE model in India on September 4. It will be offered with a 1.6-litre strong-hybrid producing 238hp and 380Nm, as well as a 2-litre diesel developing 202hp and 441Nm. The Sorento’s front end features Kia’s Tiger Nose grille, vertical LED headlights with Y-shaped DRLs, LED fog lamps and aero vents at the bumper’s outer edges. Kia has not confirmed the wheel size, but 19-inch alloys are expected. The rear gets squared tail-lights with an inverted L-shaped LED pattern, a large roof spoiler and a two-tone bumper.Inside, the dashboard uses a connected screen layout for the infotainment and instrument cluster. Both displays are expected to measure 12.3 inches, although their sizes have not been confirmed. Kia’s official images also show ADAS, ventilated front seats, a digital IRVM, a powered tailgate, dual-zone climate control, ambient lighting and a panoramic sunroof. The Sorento is expected in six- and seven-seat versions. Bookings are already open, with the SUV set to rival the Skoda Kodiaq, Volkswagen Tayron and Jeep Meridian.Maruti Baleno faceliftMaruti Suzuki is preparing to update the second-generation Baleno, which was introduced in 2022. Spy images point to a redesigned front with a new grille featuring a horizontal bar connecting the headlights. The bumper also appears to lose the fog lamps offered on the current car.At the side, the main change is expected to be a new alloy wheel design. A revised rear bumper could be added, while the tail-lights are likely to remain unchanged. The cabin is expected to retain the 9-inch touchscreen, with revised upholstery and additional features.The existing engines are likely to continue. The petrol version uses a 90hp 1.2-litre naturally aspirated engine with five-speed manual and five-speed AMT options. The 77.5hp CNG version will remain available exclusively with the manual gearbox. Rivals will continue to include the Tata Altroz, Hyundai i20 and Toyota Glanza.BMW 7 Series and i7 faceliftsBMW will launch the updated 7 Series and i7 in India on September 11. Bookings opened on August 1 following their global debut earlier this year. The Indian 7 Series range currently consists of the 740i petrol and 740d diesel, while the i7 is sold in eDrive 50 and M70 xDrive forms. BMW has not yet confirmed which variants of the updated cars it will offer here.The facelifted 740i and 740d retain their 3.0-litre straight-six engines but gain more power. The 740i now produces 400hp and 580Nm, up 19hp and 60Nm, while the 740d makes 313hp and 670Nm, an increase of 27hp and 20Nm. Both continue with 48V mild-hybrid systems, eight-speed automatic gearboxes and xDrive all-wheel drive.The i7 receives a 112.4kWh battery, replacing the previous 101.7kWh unit. The 50 variant now comes only with xDrive and makes 455hp and 660Nm, up 6hp and 10Nm. The M70 xDrive produces 680hp and 1,100Nm, gaining 30hp and 85Nm. Charging speeds have also been increased.Both models get revised styling, including split LED headlights, slimmer and taller kidney grilles with illuminated surrounds and larger bumper air intakes. Changes along the side include redesigned side skirts and alloy wheels, while the rear receives wraparound LED tail-lights, a new tailgate and revised bumper.The cabin has also been updated, with a 17.9-inch infotainment screen, 14.6-inch passenger display and BMW’s full-width Panoramic Vision display at the base of the windscreen. A four-spoke steering wheel replaces the previous design, while the centre console and transmission tunnel have been revised.Rear passengers get powered seats with heating, ventilation, massage and lumbar support. The 31.3-inch 8K Theatre Screen can now be controlled by touch, and the rear-door displays have also been updated. Other features include ambient lighting, a Bowers & Wilkins surround sound system and four-zone climate control. The 7 Series will continue to compete with the Mercedes-Benz S-Class, which was also facelifted this year.Porsche Cayenne ElectricPorsche will showcase the Cayenne Electric in India on September 30, after announcing its prices in November last year. The standard version costs Rs 1.77 crore, while the Turbo Electric is priced at Rs 2.27 crore, both ex-showroom.Both variants use a 113kWh battery and dual-motor all-wheel drive. The Turbo Electric produces 1,156hp and 1,500Nm with Launch Control and reaches 100kph from a standstill in 2.5 seconds. Its top speed is electronically limited to 260kph, while the claimed WLTP range is 537km. The standard Cayenne Electric develops 442hp and 835Nm with Launch Control. It takes 4.8 seconds to reach 100kph and has a 230kph electronically limited top speed. Its claimed WLTP range is 542km.The EV retains the overall shape of the ICE-powered Cayenne but gets a closed-off grille and two bumper-mounted air vents for cooling the battery and electrical components. The Turbo has larger vents. At the rear, a full-width LED light bar incorporates illuminated Porsche lettering, while the bumper uses horizontal black elements.The interior shares its basic layout with the ICE model, including a three-spoke steering wheel and digital driver’s display. A new 14.5-inch curved infotainment screen extends into the centre console, while a 14.9-inch passenger display is available as an option. Equipment includes eight-way electrically adjustable front seats, four-zone automatic climate control, ventilated front seats, a panoramic sunroof and wireless phone charging.

articles.title: Melinda French Gates' father worked on NASA's Apollo missions; the women engineers she met at his company picnics shaped her thinking
articles.summary: US News: Melinda French Gates grew up in a household where science, engineering and education were closely woven into family life. Her father, Raymond Joseph F.
articles.body: Melinda French Gates grew up in a household where science, engineering and education were closely woven into family life. Her father, Raymond Joseph French Jr., was an aerospace engineer whose career included work connected to NASA's Apollo programme, giving his daughter an early glimpse into the world of space exploration and advanced technology. But some of the most influential experiences from her childhood happened away from laboratories and launch sites. At company picnics connected to her father's workplace, French Gates met women who worked as engineers and mathematicians, seeing first-hand that women could build careers in technical fields. Those encounters helped shape her understanding of what was possible for women and girls, an idea that would later become a recurring theme in her own career, technology work and philanthropic efforts.Melinda French Gates' father worked on NASA's Apollo missionsRaymond French's career in aerospace placed him close to one of the most ambitious technological projects of the 20th century. He worked for the aerospace industry during the era of the Apollo programme, America's effort to send astronauts to the Moon and return them safely to Earth. For French Gates, this meant the space programme was not simply something she watched on television. Her father's work gave the family a personal connection to the engineering effort behind the missions. She has spoken about growing up in Dallas and watching Apollo launches with her family, while understanding that her father was involved in the broader aerospace world that made such missions possible. The experience exposed her from an early age to the idea that mathematics, science and engineering could be used to solve extraordinarily difficult problems.The women engineers she met became important examplesThe people French Gates encountered through her father's professional life were arguably just as influential as the technology surrounding the Apollo era. She has recalled meeting women who worked in technical positions at company picnics and other gatherings associated with her father's workplace. Her father talked about women mathematicians working on his teams and made sure his daughters could see these women as real professionals. For a young girl growing up during a period when engineering and technology were still overwhelmingly associated with men, that visibility mattered. The women were not presented as an abstract argument about equality. They were people she could meet, speak with and observe pursuing demanding careers. Seeing them helped demonstrate that technical ability and professional ambition were not limited by gender.Company picnics offered her a different view of women's careersA company picnic might seem like an ordinary family event, but for French Gates it provided an unusual form of career exposure. She could see women participating in the same professional world as her father and contributing to complex technical work. That experience mattered because children often form ideas about what careers are available to them from the people they see around them. A girl who rarely encounters women in engineering may unconsciously conclude that the field is not meant for her. French Gates instead encountered women who challenged that assumption. The lesson was subtle but powerful. Women could be mathematicians, engineers and technology professionals, and they could contribute meaningfully to some of the most challenging projects of their time.Her parents made education a priorityHer father's career was only one part of the environment that encouraged French Gates to pursue education. Her mother, Elaine French, also placed enormous importance on giving her children opportunities that she herself had not received. French Gates grew up as one of four children, and her parents expected all of them to attend university. The family worked to make higher education financially possible, reinforcing the idea that education was an investment rather than a luxury. This emphasis eventually helped lead French Gates to Duke University, where she studied computer science and economics before earning an MBA. The combination of her father's technical background and her parents' belief in education created an environment in which pursuing a demanding academic path was encouraged rather than discouraged.She eventually chose computer scienceFrench Gates' decision to study computer science gave her childhood exposure to engineering a direct connection with her own career. She attended Ursuline Academy in Dallas before going to Duke University, where she studied computer science and economics. At the time, computer science was developing rapidly but remained a field in which women were underrepresented. Her choice to enter the discipline placed her directly inside the technological world she had encountered indirectly through her father. She later joined Microsoft, where she worked in areas including product development and management. Her career demonstrated that the exposure she received as a child did not remain simply an interesting family memory. It became part of a trajectory that took her into one of the world's most influential technology companies.Apollo showed her what science could accomplishThe Apollo programme also offered a powerful lesson about collaboration and possibility. Sending astronauts to the Moon required contributions from huge numbers of scientists, engineers, mathematicians and other specialists. The programme demonstrated that seemingly impossible objectives could become achievable when people with different technical skills worked towards the same goal. Growing up around someone involved in the aerospace industry allowed French Gates to see this world at close range. The lesson extended beyond space exploration. Science and technology could be tools for solving problems, creating opportunities and expanding the boundaries of what people believed possible. That understanding would later become important in her own approach to technology and social issues.Her mother's influence reinforced the importance of opportunityFrench Gates has also credited her mother with helping shape her attitude towards education and ambition. Elaine French had not had the opportunity to attend college, and she wanted her children to have access to opportunities that had been unavailable to her. The family's focus on education therefore carried a personal meaning. French Gates was raised with the expectation that she would study, work hard and become self-sufficient. Her parents' different influences complemented one another. Her father provided an example of technical work and introduced his daughters to women working in STEM fields, while her mother emphasised the transformative power of education. Together, these experiences helped establish an early belief that opportunity should be expanded rather than restricted.From technology to a wider mission for womenFrench Gates eventually moved far beyond her career in computer science and technology. Through her philanthropic work, she became a major advocate for women and girls, focusing on areas including health, economic opportunity and access to education. Her later work has repeatedly returned to the question of what prevents women from reaching their full potential. The childhood experience of meeting women engineers provides an early illustration of why representation can matter. Seeing someone succeed in a field can make that path feel imaginable to the next generation. The women French Gates encountered through her father's workplace showed her that technical careers were possible for women. Decades later, her own work has frequently centred on helping women gain the resources and opportunities needed to pursue their own ambitions.Why seeing women in science matteredThe influence of those company picnics illustrates a broader point about how career aspirations develop. Young people do not learn only through classrooms or textbooks. They also learn from the people they encounter and the possibilities they see around them. French Gates could have grown up thinking of engineering and mathematics as overwhelmingly male professions. Instead, she met women who were already succeeding in those areas. That experience gave substance to the idea that she could enter a technical field herself. It also helped create a connection between representation and opportunity that has remained visible throughout her later advocacy. A role model does not necessarily need to deliver a formal lesson. Sometimes simply seeing someone like yourself succeeding can quietly expand the boundaries of what you believe you can become.The childhood lesson that followed her into adulthoodFrench Gates' story ultimately connects three elements that appeared early in her life: technology, education and the visibility of women in technical careers. Her father's aerospace career exposed her to the extraordinary work surrounding the Apollo era, while the women she met through his professional world demonstrated that women could contribute to that work themselves. Her parents' emphasis on education then gave her the foundation to pursue her own academic ambitions. She went on to study computer science, work at Microsoft and eventually devote much of her public life to expanding opportunities for women and girls. The women she encountered at those company gatherings may have been only one part of a much larger set of influences, but they provided a lesson that stayed with her: seeing women succeed can change what the next generation believes is possible.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Siberia’s Batagaika Crater has grown for decades as permafrost melts, exposing Ice Age animals and ancient landscapes buried for thousands of years
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Deep in northeastern Siberia, a vast scar in the landscape continues to grow as warming temperatures melt the ground that has remained frozen for thou.
articles.body: Deep in northeastern Siberia, a vast scar in the landscape continues to grow as warming temperatures melt the ground that has remained frozen for thousands of years. Known as the Batagaika Crater, and also as a massive thaw slump, the formation is the world's largest permafrost crater. Its expanding walls are exposing layers of ice, soil and organic material that offer an extraordinary record of Earth's past. According to the U.S. Geological Survey(USGS), some of the permafrost visible at the bottom may be as much as 650,000 years old. The site has also yielded remarkably preserved remains of extinct animals, while its rapidly changing shape provides a striking example of what can happen when frozen ground becomes unstable. Batagaika is therefore both a window into an ancient Siberian world and a warning about the consequences of continued permafrost thaw.Massive expanding hole revealing clues about life during the Ice AgeThe destruction of the landscape has created an unexpected opportunity for scientists. As the walls of the mega-slump retreat, they expose layers that would otherwise remain buried deep underground. The USGS describes each exposed layer as a snapshot in time. Together, these layers can help researchers investigate how the climate and environment changed over immense periods. The oldest permafrost visible near the bottom of the formation may be up to 650,000 years old. Satellite observations have also allowed scientists to follow the crater's physical expansion over decades. According to the USGS, imagery ranging from declassified satellite records collected in the 1960s to modern Landsat and Copernicus Sentinel-2 observations provides a continuous view of its growth over roughly 60 years. This makes Batagaika unusual in two ways. It is changing rapidly in the present, while simultaneously uncovering a much older record of Siberia's past. The layers exposed along its walls offer evidence of environments that existed long before modern humans began recording the planet's climate.How did the giant crater of Siberia formThe Batagaika Crater lies in Siberia's Yana Uplands and is not a crater in the usual sense of the word. It was formed when permanently frozen ground, known as permafrost, began to melt and collapse, creating what scientists call a mega-slump. Nasa's Earth Observatory explains that rising temperatures have melted the permafrost in the region. Warmer summers and shorter winters have caused layers of frozen soil and ice to collapse and erode away. The exposed face of the slope then becomes increasingly unstable, allowing the formation to move backwards into the surrounding hillside.The process can also accelerate itself. As material at the bottom melts and falls away, more frozen ground becomes exposed to warmer air. That newly exposed ground then begins to thaw(melt away), potentially causing further collapse. Nasa reported that once a feature of this scale has been exposed, stopping the process is extremely difficult. The European Space Agency(ESA), described the formation in May 2026 as the world's biggest permafrost crater. The agency said the crater is roughly 100 metres deep and around one kilometre long, and has been growing at approximately 30 metres per year. ESA linked its rapid expansion to warmer temperatures and deforestation, both of which have helped destabilise the frozen ground.Ice Age animals emerging from the frozen ground in SiberiaBatagaika's frozen deposits have also preserved traces of animals that lived during the Ice Age. The USGS notes that mummified wildlife has been discovered at the site, including the remains of a ‘42,000-year-old foal’ belonging to an extinct horse species, found in 2018. Nasa has reported other remarkable discoveries from the expanding crater. Remains of the ‘extinct Lena horse’ and ‘prehistoric steppe bison’ have emerged from the melting ground, alongside remains associated with cave lions and wolves. These discoveries provide scientists with physical evidence of the animals that once lived in this part of Siberia.The ancient deposits also preserve evidence of changing vegetation. Nasa reported that pieces of wood found in the melting soil suggest spruce and pine forests once grew in the area, while research at the site has indicated that the region experienced periods with different climatic conditions. Today, however, the landscape surrounding the crater is dominated by low shrubs and larch trees. The growing hole is, in effect, exposing fragments of ecosystems that disappeared thousands of years ago.Why is the crater's growth also a climate warningBatagaika's scientific value comes with a serious environmental concern. Permafrost contains large amounts of frozen organic material, and when the ground melts, the carbon stored within it can begin to enter the atmosphere. The USGS warns that thawing permafrost soils can release greenhouse gases, including carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide, which contribute to global warming. This means the expanding crater is not simply a consequence of a warming climate; the melting process itself may contribute to further warming.The site's striking appearance has often drawn attention from satellites. ESA says the crater resembles a tadpole or stingray when viewed from above. Yet behind that unusual image is a landscape undergoing rapid and continuing change. Batagaika presents a remarkable scientific contradiction. Its growth is destroying ancient frozen ground, but that destruction is also revealing a record of landscapes, climates and animals from hundreds of thousands of years ago. The deeper it expands, the more of that ancient world becomes visible while the continued melting offers a stark reminder that Earth's coldest landscapes are changing in real time.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: DEHRADUN: Heavy overnight rainfall in Dehradun and adjoining areas caused the Tamasa River, which flows through the premises of the historic Shri Tapk.
articles.body: DEHRADUN: Heavy overnight rainfall in Dehradun and adjoining areas caused the Tamasa River, which flows through the premises of the historic Shri Tapkeshwar Mahadev Temple, to swell significantly, local officials said on Tuesday.The torrential rains across northern India have led to flood-like conditions along several major river basins, affecting multiple districts in Uttarakhand and Uttar Pradesh.In Uttar Pradesh's Prayagraj, rising water levels in both the Ganga and Yamuna rivers forced floodwaters into residential settlements along the riverbanks, causing distress among residents and prompting municipal authorities to keep response teams on alert.Similarly, in Varanasi, the water level of the Ganga River has been continuously rising due to sustained heavy rainfall upstream, inundating low-lying areas and disrupting routine activity along the city's prominent ghats.Local administrations across the affected regions are closely monitoring the situation, with emergency service personnel deployed near riverbanks to prevent any untoward incidents.Meanwhile, all government, private, and non-government schools from Classes 1 to 12 as well as Anganwadi centres in Dehradun district will remain closed on Tuesday in view of the forecast for heavy to very heavy rainfall, lightning, and extremely heavy spells of rain in parts of the district, officials told news agency ANI.The one-day holiday was declared by Dehradun District Magistrate and District Disaster Management Authority chairperson as a precautionary measure following the issuance of an Orange alert.According to the order issued on August 31, the latest weather forecast and nowcast indicated the possibility of severe weather conditions over the next 24 hours.The Chief Education Officer and District Programme Officer, Dehradun, have been directed to ensure strict compliance with the order across all educational institutions.Meanwhile, the water level of the Ganga in Rishikesh has risen amid continuous heavy rainfall in the hilly areas of the Garhwal division, though the river remains below the warning mark, officials said.The Ganga was flowing swiftly at Triveni Ghat. However, officials from the Central Water Commission said the river level was still within the normal range and below the danger threshold.Amid rising water levels, teams from the State Disaster Response Force (SDRF), Water Police and Disaster Relief Teams have been deployed at major ghats across Rishikesh, Muni Ki Reti and Lakshman Jhula.Emergency personnel are also making regular announcements over loudspeakers, urging devotees, tourists and local residents to exercise caution and stay away from the riverbanks. articles.title: In 1985, Harrison Ford began protecting 389 acres of his 800-acre Wyoming ranch from development, preserving a migration corridor for elk and mule deer
articles.summary: US News: Harrison Ford bought an 800-acre property in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, after he decided that the valley suited him better than Sun Valley. Elk and mule d.
articles.body: Harrison Ford bought an 800-acre property in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, after he decided that the valley suited him better than Sun Valley. Elk and mule deer already moved across the ranch, while bald eagles, blue herons and native cutthroat trout occupied parts of the property. Ford later began placing conservation easements on the land to limit development. By the 1990s, 389 acres of Ford’s ranch had been placed into a perpetual conservation easement, and the arrangement prevented the protected portion from being developed and kept the land available as wildlife habitat.Ford chose the entire 800-acre propertyFord and his then-wife, Melissa Mathison, were looking for a place outside Los Angeles in the early 1980s, and initially considered properties around Sun Valley before turning their attention to Jackson Hole. The property they eventually selected covered 800 acres along the Snake River. The Land Report says migrating elk and mule deer used the pastures, while the property also supported bald eagles, blue herons and native cutthroat trout.Ford had the option of buying only the existing house and a small surrounding parcel, but instead purchased the entire tract. He designed the main house later while working in Paris on the film Frantic, sending instructions to workers in Wyoming. A 1994 Los Angeles Times profile described the property as an 800-acre ranch with a family compound, guest cottages, a workshop and areas of spruce, aspen and hawthorn.Conservation easements changed what could be builtFord began donating conservation easements on his property in 1985, according to the Land Report. The easements prohibited substantial development or other development that would impair wildlife and natural resources on the protected portions of the ranch. A conservation easement places permanent restrictions on how the land can be developed, and in Jackson Hole, such easements have become an important tool for keeping private parcels connected to surrounding wildlife habitat. The Jackson Hole Land Trust now says conservation easements are particularly important in Teton County because private land is concentrated on the valley floor, where wildlife depends on open areas and connected habitat.389 acres were placed in perpetual protectionFord had placed 389 acres of his 800-acre ranch into perpetual trust as wildlife habitat by August 1994, according to the Los Angeles Times. The newspaper reported that Ford planned to use only a few additional small areas for possible homes for his children. The protected acreage represented nearly half of the ranch, which also covered land that wildlife already used. The Los Angeles Times described elk and other animals that moved through the property, while the Land Report specifically noted the presence of migrating elk and mule deer. Conservation easements were still relatively uncommon when Ford's decision came, and the Land Report quoted Stephen Small, who helped write the federal tax provisions governing conservation easements, as saying that the Jackson Hole Land Trust was an early pioneer in the field.The land became part of Ford's conservation workFord was interested in protecting the ranch for broader involvement in environmental conservation, and he served on the board of Conservation International and later became vice chair of the organization. XPRIZE's biography of Ford notes that he donated 389 acres of his Wyoming property to the Jackson Hole Land Trust for a conservation easement. It also describes his long involvement with Conservation International and its biodiversity programs.The Land Report said Ford's conservation work on his own property was closely connected to his interest in environmental protection elsewhere. His Jackson Hole ranch, however, provided a direct way to restrict development on land where wildlife was already moving.Elk and mule deer still depend on connected habitatElk and mule deer move between seasonal ranges across a mixture of public and private land, which make undeveloped private parcels important where they connect larger habitat areas. The Wyoming Wildlife Federation identifies migration corridors as critical areas that allow elk, mule deer and other ungulates to move between summer and winter ranges.Ford's 389-acre easement has a rather narrow role: it permanently restricts development on part of an 800-acre private ranch that lies within a landscape used by wildlife. The Jackson Hole Land Trust currently lists more than 20,000 acres of protected land in the Jackson Hole area, with elk, moose, mule deer and pronghorn among the wildlife species associated with those conservation areas.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2012, a derelict 1866 Washington house was listed on a waterfront lot worth more without it; preservationists spent 6 years buying it and 8 more restoring it before reopening it in 2026
articles.summary: US News: In 2012, a crumbling 1866 farmhouse sat on a prized waterfront lot in Coupeville, Washington, listed for sale at a price that reflected the land’s val.
articles.body: In 2012, a crumbling 1866 farmhouse sat on a prized waterfront lot in Coupeville, Washington, listed for sale at a price that reflected the land’s value far more than the building’s. The Haller House, one of the oldest surviving structures on Whidbey Island, was in such poor condition that many assumed it would be demolished to make way for a new home. Instead, a group of local preservationists stepped in, spending six years raising funds and negotiating to save the house, then another eight years carefully restoring it. In 2026, the Haller House finally reopened to the public as a museum and community space, a testament to what can happen when a community decides a piece of its history is worth fighting for, according to updates and historical accounts from Historic Whidbey, the nonprofit that led the rescue and restoration.A house older than the state itselfThe Haller House was built in 1866 by early settlers on Whidbey Island, just a few years after the Civil War and three decades before Washington became a state. Originally a modest farmhouse, it grew over time as the family expanded, adding rooms and outbuildings that reflected changing needs and tastes.For more than a century, the house stood as a quiet witness to the island’s transformation: from logging and farming to tourism and commuter communities. But by the early 2000s, years of neglect, water damage and deferred maintenance had left the structure in serious trouble. Roofs leaked, foundations shifted, and parts of the framing were compromised. To many observers, the house looked like a lost cause.The moment it almost disappearedIn 2012, the Haller House and its waterfront lot came up for sale. The asking price was driven largely by the value of the land, with its views of Penn Cove and proximity to Coupeville’s historic downtown. From a purely financial perspective, it made more sense to tear down the house and build something new than to try to save it.For Historic Whidbey, a local preservation nonprofit, the listing was a warning bell. If the house was lost, one of the last tangible links to the island’s earliest Euro-American settlement would disappear. The organisation began exploring whether it could purchase the property, even though it lacked the funds at the time.Six years to secure the houseWhat followed was a long, uncertain campaign to raise money and build support. Historic Whidbey worked with donors, grant-making organisations and community members to piece together enough capital to buy the Haller House and its lot. The effort included: Fundraising events and membership drives; applications for state and private preservation grants; and outreach to residents who remembered the house from childhood or had family connections to it.In 2018, six years after the house first appeared on the market, Historic Whidbey finally completed the purchase. By then, the building had deteriorated further, and the real work was only beginning.Eight years of careful restorationRestoring the Haller House was not a simple renovation. The goal was to stabilise the structure, repair or replace damaged elements and return the house to a condition that reflected its historical character while making it safe and accessible for visitors.Key phases of the work included: Structural repairs to foundations, sills and framing to stop ongoing movement and decay; roof replacement and drainage improvements to prevent future water damage; careful removal of later additions and alterations that obscured the house’s original layout; restoration of historic windows, doors, mouldings and finishes using period-appropriate materials and techniques; and installation of modern systems—electrical, plumbing, heating and fire protection—in ways that minimised visual impact.Throughout the process, volunteers and staff documented the house’s construction phases, salvaged original materials where possible and consulted historical records to guide decisions. The work stretched over eight years, with progress sometimes slowed by funding gaps, weather and the sheer complexity of working with an aging, hand-built structure.Reopening in 2026 as a community resourceIn 2026, the Haller House finally reopened its doors. No longer a derelict eyesore or a private residence, it now serves as a museum and community space operated by Historic Whidbey. Visitors can tour the restored rooms, learn about the families who lived there and explore exhibits on Whidbey Island’s early history, from Indigenous use of the land to pioneer settlement and maritime industries.The house also hosts educational programs, lectures and special events that connect residents and visitors to the island’s heritage. For a community that has grown rapidly in recent decades, the Haller House offers a physical anchor to the past, a place where people can touch the same woodwork, walk the same floors and look out the same windows as those who built the community more than 150 years ago.Why this kind of preservation mattersThe Haller House story is unusual in its scale and timeline. Still, it reflects a broader truth about historic preservation: saving old buildings is often harder, slower and more expensive than it looks from the outside. It requires patience, sustained funding and a willingness to accept that some projects will take decades.For Whidbey Island, the payoff is a tangible link to its origins. In a region where many historic structures have been lost to fire, redevelopment or neglect, the Haller House stands as proof that communities can choose a different path. It also demonstrates how a single building can become a catalyst for broader interest in local history, inspiring people to learn more about the landscapes, industries and cultures that shaped the place they call home.A model for other small communitiesHistoric Whidbey’s approach, combining grassroots fundraising, professional restoration and long-term stewardship, offers a model for other small towns and rural areas facing similar choices. Not every old house can or should be saved, but when a building carries exceptional historical value and community support, projects like the Haller House show what is possible.Today, the house is more than a restored structure; it is a symbol of what a community can accomplish when it decides that its history is worth investing in. From a derelict 1866 farmhouse on a valuable waterfront lot to a reopened museum in 2026, the Haller House’s second life is a reminder that some stories are worth waiting for.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
